passage: "Damini didi, you know when Nanu died last winter? Everyone kept telling me, 'Darshan, he's in a better place,' and I kept thinking, how do they know? I wasn't angry exactly. Just... it cracked something open. Where did he go? Does anything I do matter if we all end? I started reading at night, anything I could find: old stories from the Upanishads, a book on black holes, even Nanu's own diary in Gujarati, which took ages. I sat in the temple some evenings and in the library some afternoons. I don't have answers. Some days that scares me. Other days it feels exciting, like I'm allowed to decide what I believe instead of just copying. Is that weird? You're the only one I can say this to."

qa.q: Whose diary did Darshan read?
qa.a: Nanu's own diary, written in Gujarati.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Darshan describe about not having answers?
qa.a: Some days the uncertainty scares Darshan, while on other days it feels exciting because Darshan gets to decide what he believes.

qa.q: What could Damini say to support Darshan?
qa.a: She could tell Darshan these questions are normal and worth having, listen without rushing to answers, and maybe share what she herself wonders about.

qa.q: How might Darshan's parents feel if they knew about the reading?
qa.a: They might be moved that Darshan is honouring Nanu, or uneasy about the questioning of what the family says, depending on how they see such doubts.

grounding: A teen tells an older didi how a loss started a search for meaning, faith and a personal philosophy.

passage: Sahil used to be the loudest one on our cricket team, always joking. This year Pankaj, that's me, noticed he'd changed. In physics, when Sir mentioned the universe was expanding, Sahil asked, "Expanding into what?" and then, "Why is there anything at all?" The class laughed. He didn't. After school he started staying back in the library with thick books from the philosophy shelf. On Sundays I saw him at the gurdwara, not just eating langar like before but serving it, quiet and focused. Once I asked him if something was wrong. He said, "No, I just want to know what I'm for." I didn't really get it. I still don't know if he's happy or worried. But he seems more awake than before, like he's listening for something.

qa.q: What did Sahil ask when the physics teacher said the universe was expanding?
qa.a: He asked what it was expanding into, and then why there is anything at all.

qa.q: What does Sahil's reply, 'I just want to know what I'm for,' suggest about his mind?
qa.a: He seems curious and searching for purpose, taking big questions about his place in the world seriously rather than as a joke.

qa.q: How could the physics teacher encourage Sahil's questions?
qa.a: He could welcome them, point him to readable books, or give time after class to talk, instead of letting the class laugh them away.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see his friend's change?
qa.a: He is puzzled and unsure whether Sahil is happy or worried, but he notices Sahil seems more awake and focused.

grounding: A friend observes a teen exploring deep questions of existence and purpose through study and spiritual practice.

passage:
First Sunday: Jasleen stood through the morning prayer at the gurdwara, thinking mostly about her maths test, the words washing past her like traffic.

The next Thursday: On a school visit to an old-age home, an old man with shaky hands held hers and asked, "Beta, what are you living for?" She laughed nervously. She had no answer. On the bus back she stared out of the window, the question stuck in her ribs.

A month later: Her notebook was titled "Things I Believe (So Far)". It had bits of Gurbani, a line from a science book about atoms made in stars, and crossed-out pages. Shankar, who called himself an atheist, argued with her at recess. "You can't prove any of it." "Maybe not," she said. "But I'm allowed to look."

qa.q: What was the title of Jasleen's notebook a month later?
qa.a: It was titled 'Things I Believe (So Far)'.

qa.q: Why did the old man's question stay with Jasleen?
qa.a: She realised she had never thought about her purpose, and not having an answer unsettled her and made her want to search.

qa.q: What small step helped Jasleen explore these questions?
qa.a: Keeping a notebook where she could collect ideas from faith and science, and cross things out as her thinking changed.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Jasleen's search?
qa.a: As an atheist he doubts her ideas can be proven, but by arguing at recess he is also taking her questions seriously.

grounding: Shows over several weeks a teen moving from routine ritual to actively exploring meaning, belief and purpose.

passage: 'You ask big questions at night, Sunaina, just like I did,' said Darshan Dada, settling his shawl. 'At sixteen I used to sleep on the roof in summer, and I would look at the stars and feel very small. What is all this for? Why am I here and not some other boy? I asked the priest at our temple, and he gave me one answer. I asked my science teacher, and she gave me another. I asked my friend the potter, who never went to school, and he said, "I don't know. But when I shape a pot, I feel joined to something." I kept all three answers for years. I still don't have just one. But I stopped being afraid of the question. It kept me company.'

qa.q: Where did young Darshan sleep in summer?
qa.a: On the roof.

qa.q: How did young Darshan feel looking at the stars?
qa.a: He felt very small and full of questions about why he existed.

qa.q: What could Sunaina take from how Darshan Dada handled these questions?
qa.a: Sunaina could ask different trusted people, keep their answers, and let the question be company rather than something scary.

qa.q: How does the potter's answer differ from the other two?
qa.a: It comes from feeling and daily work rather than teaching or scripture, showing meaning can be found in doing.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring questions of existence by gathering spiritual, scientific and personal answers.

passage: Yamini had planned the sunrise walk with Ritu for weeks, but at five Ritu texted that she had a fever and couldn't come. Yamini went up the hill behind the town alone. Fog swallowed the view; there would be no sunrise. She sat on the wet bench anyway, annoyed, hood up. Lately every question in her head ended the same way: what is the point of any of it, marks, college, even being kind? Her family prayed every evening; her best friend believed in nothing she could name. Yamini didn't know where she stood. In the fog she could hear a temple bell below, a dog, someone's pressure cooker. For one strange second she felt part of all of it. She typed to Ritu: 'No sunrise. But something. Tell you later.'

qa.q: Why couldn't Ritu come on the walk?
qa.a: She had a fever.

qa.q: What did Yamini feel for 'one strange second' in the fog?
qa.a: She felt connected to everything around her, a sense of belonging her questions hadn't given her.

qa.q: What might help Yamini keep exploring these questions?
qa.a: Talking them over with Ritu, her family or a teacher she trusts, and reading different views, without rushing to settle on one.

qa.q: How might Ritu react to the message 'No sunrise. But something'?
qa.a: She would probably be curious and a bit sorry she missed it, and keen to hear what Yamini meant.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager wrestling with questions of purpose and glimpsing a feeling of universal connection on a foggy morning.

passage: On the terrace of their Pune building, Tushar, sixteen, lay on a mat beside his grandmother Madhuri, watching stars. "Aaji, what do you think we're here for?" She didn't answer right away. "When I was your age, I thought it was to do my duty. Later, I thought it was to love my children. Now I think it's to pay attention." "To what?" "To this." She pointed at the sky, then at him. Tushar was quiet. He'd been reading about the universe, how tiny Earth was, and it frightened him. But lying there, it felt less like being tiny and more like being part of something. He wrote her words in his phone's notes that night.

qa.q: Where were Tushar and his grandmother lying?
qa.a: On the terrace of their Pune building.

qa.q: How did Tushar's feeling about being tiny change?
qa.a: It went from frightening to feeling connected, as if he was part of something bigger.

qa.q: What might help Tushar keep exploring these questions?
qa.a: Keep talking with people like Aaji, reading widely and writing down his own thoughts.

qa.q: How might Aaji Madhuri feel about Tushar's question?
qa.a: Touched and glad, seeing him think deeply about life.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring questions of meaning and connection with his grandmother.

passage:
"Kavitha, do you ever feel like the hills are listening?"
"Lalremsiami, it's six in the morning. I feel like sleeping."
"I'm serious." Lalremsiami, sixteen, pulled her shawl tighter. "At church, I feel close to God. But up here, I feel it too, and there's no church."
"Maybe God's not only in buildings."
"You don't even believe in a God."
"I believe in something," Kavitha said. "When my grandmother died, I felt like she went back into everything. The trees, the rain."
"That's beautiful."
"So maybe we're both looking at the same thing from different sides."
They watched the mist lift off the valley, and neither spoke for a long time.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami pull tighter?
qa.a: Her shawl.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling on the hill?
qa.a: She felt a deep sense of closeness and wonder, as if connected to something beyond herself.

qa.q: What made this conversation work despite their different beliefs?
qa.a: Both listened with respect and looked for what they shared rather than who was right.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel sharing her thoughts about her grandmother?
qa.a: Tender and a bit exposed, but glad Lalremsiami found it beautiful.

grounding: Shows two teenagers exploring spiritual questions and universal connection from different beliefs.

passage: I'm Ritu. When I was seventeen, I went on a trek with my school to a village in the hills, and our guide was an old farmer named Bhupen. On the last night I asked him if he ever wondered what life was for. He laughed. "Every morning," he said. "Then I water the apple trees." I thought it was a joke. But on the long bus home I kept thinking about it: maybe meaning isn't one big answer, but what you choose to care for each day. I started keeping a notebook of questions I didn't have answers to. It's still growing.

qa.q: What does Bhupen do every morning after wondering?
qa.a: He waters the apple trees.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel about Bhupen's answer at first?
qa.a: Ritu thought it was a joke and felt a little puzzled, before it began to feel meaningful.

qa.q: What turning point shaped Ritu's personal philosophy?
qa.a: Thinking about Bhupen's answer on the bus, and seeing meaning as daily care rather than one big answer.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen Ritu's question?
qa.a: With amusement and kindness, as a question he still lives with himself.

grounding: Shows a teenager exploring questions of meaning and forming a personal philosophy after a conversation with a farmer.

passage:
Nature camp note, Night 3. Irfan Qureshi, camp mentor.
After the campfire, Ayesha, fifteen, stayed out on the rock looking at the stars. When I checked on her, she asked, "Do you think we're here for a reason, or is it just chance?" I asked what she thought. She said sometimes she feels part of everything, the trees, the people back home, even the stars, and other times she feels tiny and pointless. We talked for twenty minutes about how different traditions and thinkers answer that question. She said she'd been reading both her grandfather's Sufi poems and a science book on the universe, and they didn't feel as far apart as she expected. I suggested she keep a notebook of her questions. She has already started.

qa.q: On which night of camp did this happen?
qa.a: Night 3.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling as she looked at the stars?
qa.a: She felt a mix of wonder and connection, and also a sense of being tiny.

qa.q: What did Irfan Qureshi suggest, and why is it a good idea?
qa.a: Keeping a notebook of her questions, so she can explore them over time without needing quick answers.

qa.q: How might Irfan Qureshi have felt being asked such a big question?
qa.a: He likely felt moved and respectful, taking care not to give her a ready-made answer.

grounding: A camp mentor's note records a teenager exploring questions of existence, connection and meaning.

passage:
Tuesday. Parul's diary.
I sat with Anand Dadu on the terrace after dinner. He's eighty-one. I asked him what he thinks life is for. I thought he'd say something from the scriptures. He said, "For a long time I thought it was to earn and build. Now I think it's to be useful to someone, and to notice things." Then he pointed at the moon and said nothing for five minutes. I kept thinking about it in bed. What would I be useful for? What do I notice? I think I notice people who are left out. Maybe that's a start. It's weird: I felt small and big at the same time.

qa.q: How old is Anand Dadu?
qa.a: Eighty-one.

qa.q: How did Parul feel lying in bed after the talk?
qa.a: Parul felt thoughtful and moved, both small and big at the same time.

qa.q: What could Parul do to explore the idea of being useful?
qa.a: Parul could act on noticing people who are left out, for example by reaching out to one of them.

qa.q: How might Anand Dadu feel about Parul's question?
qa.a: He likely felt touched that his grandchild asked, and took it seriously.

grounding: A teenager's diary records asking a grandfather about life's purpose and starting to form a personal answer.

passage:
On the night of the village jatra, Yamini climbed the old water tank with her friend Farida instead of watching the drama. Below them the fair glowed; above them the sky was thick with stars she never saw in the town where she studied.
"Do you ever think we're just dust that learned to think?" Yamini said.
Farida laughed. "Only you would say that at a jatra."
"I mean it. Then why does anything matter? Why does Amma pray every morning? Why do I want to be a teacher?"
Farida thought for a while. "Maybe it matters because we're here together for a bit."
Yamini lay back on the cold concrete. She didn't have an answer. But she felt, for a second, very small and very connected, both at once.

qa.q: Where did Yamini and Farida climb?
qa.a: The old water tank.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling as she lay on the concrete?
qa.a: She felt small and connected at the same time, full of wonder without an answer.

qa.q: How could a trusted adult respond if Yamini brought these questions home?
qa.a: They could listen and share their own view, like why Amma prays, without insisting she agree.

qa.q: How does Farida see Yamini's big question?
qa.a: Farida is amused at first but then takes it seriously and offers her own gentle answer.

grounding: Shows a teen exploring questions about existence and meaning under the stars.

passage:
Ulla's grandmother died in March, and by June Ulla still hadn't cried at the right times. At the Swedish summer camp, she sat on the jetty every evening, feet in the cold lake, asking herself where people go.
Tuan, the quiet boy from her cabin, sat down one night with a torch. "My family lights incense for our ancestors. My mum says they're still with us."
"Do you believe that?"
"Some days. Other days I think they're just in how we do things. My grandfather folded his shirts a weird way. I do too."
Ulla thought about her grandmother humming while she baked.
"Maybe she's in the humming," Ulla said.
They sat there until the midges came out. It wasn't an answer. It felt like the start of one.

qa.q: Where did Ulla sit every evening?
qa.a: On the jetty, with her feet in the cold lake.

qa.q: How was Ulla feeling at the camp?
qa.a: She felt lost and quietly grieving, unsure where people go after they die.

qa.q: How did Tuan help Ulla think about meaning?
qa.a: He shared his family's belief and his own doubts without pushing, giving Ulla room to find her own idea.

qa.q: What might Tuan be feeling when he talks about his grandfather's shirts?
qa.a: Tuan may feel a warm, slightly shy connection to his grandfather, sharing something private.

grounding: Shows a teen exploring questions about death, connection and meaning with a friend.

passage:
In the school's philosophy club, which met in the chemistry lab after hours, the question that Friday was "What is a good life?"
Amandeep said a good life was money and family. Someone else said faith. Anirban, who usually argued with everyone, was quiet.
The teacher asked him directly.
"I don't know," Anirban said. "My father prays. My mother doesn't. They're both good. So maybe it's not what you believe, it's how you live?"
Amandeep frowned. "But then what's the point of believing anything?"
Anirban shrugged. "Maybe believing helps some people live well. I'm still looking for what helps me."
Walking out, Amandeep said, "You're annoying. But I'm going to think about that all weekend."

qa.q: Where did the philosophy club meet?
qa.a: In the chemistry lab after hours.

qa.q: What might Anirban have been feeling before he answered?
qa.a: He may have felt uncertain and thoughtful, still unsure what he believed.

qa.q: How could the teacher build on Anirban's idea next week?
qa.a: The teacher could ask each student to name one way they want to live and what helps them, whatever their belief.

qa.q: How is Amandeep affected by Anirban's answer?
qa.a: Amandeep is frustrated at first but intrigued, saying he'll think about it all weekend.

grounding: Shows teens exploring personal philosophy and spiritual orientation in a school club.

passage:
Dear Imran,
Remember how we used to lie on the terrace naming stars? Last night the power went out and I did it alone. I kept thinking: that light is millions of years old, and I'm stressing about entrance exams. Does any of it matter? And then, strangely, it did. I felt tiny but also connected to everything, like I'm made of the same stuff as that light. I asked Dadi what she believes, and she said she prays not for answers but to feel less alone with the questions. I'm not sure I believe what she believes. But I want a way to find that terrace feeling more often. Maybe I'll write to you from the terrace every Sunday. Tell me what you think about when you can't sleep.
Pallavi

qa.q: What did Pallavi and Imran use to do on the terrace?
qa.a: They used to lie on the terrace naming stars.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel looking at the stars alone?
qa.a: Pallavi felt tiny but also connected to everything, a mix of awe and calm after the worry about exams.

qa.q: What small practice could help Pallavi keep exploring these questions?
qa.a: Writing from the terrace every Sunday, and keeping the conversation going with Dadi and Imran, gives the questions a regular place.

qa.q: How does Dadi approach the big questions?
qa.a: Dadi prays not for answers but to feel less alone with the questions, finding comfort in faith rather than certainty.

grounding: Shows a teenager wondering about existence and connection, and exploring a grandmother's spiritual view.
